title: Blood Dazzler: opening poems
subtitle: Patricia Smith · pp. vii–24

scope.exclude: All of What to Tweak, beginning on p. 25

frequency.title: Repeated words
frequency.lead: These are ten frequently repeated words worth tracking. Frequency tells us what returns; interpretation explains what changes.

words.note: Ordinary weather becomes something familiar, beautiful, or dangerous; repetition also shapes Ghazal.
A repeated instruction means different things to people with different choices.
Small possessions, pleasures, bodies, and comforts face a much larger storm.
Necessary water and threatening water recur together.
Speakers claim knowledge, question it, or confront what they cannot predict.
A name can identify a place, confer power, or claim authority.
A familiar hat color becomes a storm color and the color of a sound.
The storm feature becomes a hungry observer.
A storm can be heard before it is understood; repeated sound becomes color.
A home is both a structure and a life made there.

frequency.pronoun_note: Pronouns also recur often. Each new poem can change who I, my, you, we, she, or it refers to.
frequency.method: 3,117 words in the poem bodies on pp. vii–24. Titles, headnotes, epigraphs, timestamps, and page numbers are excluded. Capitalization is ignored; contractions and hyphenated words remain intact; straight and curly apostrophes are treated alike. These are selected exact-word counts, not totals for word families.

key_words.student: Water can attract, sustain, delight, or destroy. Identify the speaker before deciding what it means.
A command to leave does not supply transport, a destination, or a reason to trust the warning. Compare the people who hear it.
A house holds inheritance, food, routine, and belongings. Money changes the choices available to its owner.
Naming Katrina gives the storm a speaking identity. Words later struggle to communicate what people need.

key_words.cluster: I · my · we · you · she · it
key_words.student: These words identify a point of view. Ask who speaks, who is addressed, and who is being described.
Smith gives the city, storm, and buildings body parts. Compare their power with the exposed human and animal bodies.
Seeing and hearing do not always produce understanding. Purple gives sound the language of color.
Religious words can express authority, hope, habit, or a question about protection. Identify which use appears in each poem.
Race and money shape warnings, movement, and the ways people are represented. Wealth is stated in “Inconvenient”; the speaker’s race is not.

characters.lead: An explicit character appears in the words of a poem. An implicit character is a person or institution we infer from an action, object, or system. The groups below keep separate unnamed speakers separate.

explicit.name: New Orleans
explicit.role: A personified city addressed as a woman. Visitors also appear in the city poems.

explicit.name: Katrina
explicit.role: The hurricane becomes a speaking woman with a mouth, eye, appetite, and desire for recognition.

explicit.name: Residents who hear, question, or resist the warning
explicit.role: Different unnamed voices describe attachment to home, barriers to leaving, and confidence from surviving an earlier storm.

explicit.name: The man on television
explicit.role: An evacuation warning reaches people through his voice.

explicit.name: The affluent evacuee and husband
explicit.role: An unnamed speaker narrates departure in a Lincoln toward another home; the speaker’s husband prepares the house.

explicit.name: Luther B, m’dear, and the departing household
explicit.role: Luther B is the dog left tied to a tree. M’dear is remembered through her care, speech, and food.

explicit.name: B-boys, children, and mothers
explicit.role: Children first treat rain as familiar; mothers later bring their lives onto rooftops.

explicit.name: The church community and its religious references
explicit.role: A choir, elders, and a preacher appear on p. 17. God, Jesus, and the Lord are invoked across the poems.

explicit.name: President George Bush and the woman in the Ninth
explicit.role: The president plays guitar while a woman voices abandonment. The headnote also names country singer Mark Willis (as printed).

explicit.name: People on the roof and helicopter crews
explicit.role: People signal, call for help, hold babies, and face rescue decisions. Aircraft noise competes with their words.

explicit.name: Tourists and unnamed sexual partners
explicit.role: Visitors seek pleasure in the city. The love-spell poem gives desire a physical, potentially violent force.

explicit.name: Mutts, priestesses, and tree trunks
explicit.role: They hear the first sound. Smith extends perception beyond the usual human witnesses.

implicit.name: Unseen camera workers and viewers
implicit.role: Cameras and judgments imply people who frame, circulate, and interpret the survivors’ images.

implicit.name: The people responsible for evacuation and protective infrastructure
implicit.role: A warning and cracking levees imply decisions about movement, protection, and public responsibility.

implicit.name: Racially prejudiced viewers
implicit.role: The focus on hair, jewelry, bodies, and speech suggests viewers who judge the survivors through stereotypes. This is an interpretation of the camera’s attention.

implicit.name: Ancestors subjected to deadly passage over water
implicit.role: Water’s earlier passage toward death suggests historical memory, possibly the Middle Passage. No ancestor or historical event is named.

discussion.title: Map: place and movement
steps: Locate the Mississippi River, Lake Pontchartrain, Industrial Canal, and Lower Ninth Ward.
Identify two obstacles to leaving in Man on the TV Say and two resources available in Inconvenient.
Explain one detail the map helps you understand and one detail it cannot tell you about either household.

discussion.title: Photographs: signals from a roof
steps: Describe two visible details in one roof photograph.
Match each detail to a word or action in Up on the Roof.
Identify one feeling, motive, or judgment in the poem that the photograph alone cannot prove.

discussion.title: Video: who can hear whom
steps: Describe the helicopter video’s camera position and one audible sound.
Find the passage in Up on the Roof where aircraft noise interferes with speech.
Explain how the poem’s you changes your position compared with the video camera’s position.

discussion.title: Compare: the same command
steps: Read the first Go in each poem aloud.
Name the speaker, a resource, and an obstacle in each poem.
Explain one change in the command’s meaning using a detail from each poem.

source_note: Reading: Patricia Smith, Blood Dazzler (Coffee House Press, 2008), pp. vii–24. All page references use the book’s printed pages.
